messages.text: She smiled. It was a small smile, barely a curve at the corner of her lips, but it transformed her face entirely. The distant, cryptic girl from the cafeteria became suddenly, startlingly human.

messages.name: Kazuhiko
messages.text: "So I have been told," I admitted.
Mei closed her book and set it on the table between us. The leather cover was embossed with a symbol I did not recognize — a circle intersected by a diagonal line, like a stylized eye.

messages.name: Mei
messages.text: "My grandmother gave me this book. She said it contains all the answers I would ever need. But I have read it three times, cover to cover, and I still do not understand half of it."

messages.name: Kazuhiko
messages.text: "Maybe the answers are not in the book," I said, surprising myself. "Maybe they are in the reading."
She tilted her head, considering this.

messages.name: Mei
messages.text: "That is either very profound or very stupid. I have not decided which."

messages.name: Kazuhiko
messages.text: "Let me know when you figure it out."

For the first time since we had met, Mei laughed. It was a quiet laugh, barely more than a breath, but it was real. And in that moment, sitting across from each other in the dusty silence of the library, something shifted between us — an invisible thread connecting two solitary people who had both been looking for somewhere to belong.

messages.name: Mei
messages.text: "From the others." She picked up her book and stood, preparing to leave. "I will see you tomorrow, Kazuhiko."

And then she was gone, her footsteps fading into the creaks and whispers of the old library, leaving me alone with a poetry book I still was not reading and a question I could not quite formulate. I felt an awkward knot in my stomach, unsure if I had said something wrong. Glancing out the window, I noticed the river bank beyond the campus, its edge littered with autumn leaves, and I wondered if she would ever reveal what lay beneath her cryptic smile.
